Based on the search results, several plants listed in the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources' invasive species reports are from the family **Asteraceae** (also known as the aster or sunflower family). 

Key Asteraceae family invasive plants documented in Wisconsin's invasive species lists include:

1. **Spotted Knapweed** (*Centaurea stoebe*, including subspecies *C. maculosa* and *C. biebersteinii*) - This species is particularly problematic in Wisconsin's sandy soils, dunes, prairies, and barrens. It belongs to the Asteraceae family and appears in Wisconsin's NR 40 invasive species regulations.

2. **Canada Thistle** (*Cirsium arvense*) - A perennial weed in the Asteraceae family that spreads aggressively through root systems.

3. **European Marsh Thistle** (*Cirsium palustre*) - Another Asteraceae member found in Wisconsin roadsides, wetlands, and forest edges.

4. **Common Tansy** (*Tanacetum vulgare*) - An herbaceous perennial in the Asteraceae family restricted to certain areas of Wisconsin (particularly Great Lakes beaches).

These plants were all part of Wisconsin DNR's invasive plant identification and management guidance during the 2020-2021 reporting period, as evidenced by their inclusion in state field guides, regulatory lists (NR 40), and monitoring programs like WISTIPP (Wisconsin Terrestrial Invasive Species Identification & Prevention Program).

Spotted knapweed is a serious invader of sunny sites and is especially troublesome in Wisconsin on sandy sites of low productivity, including grasslands, barrens and great lakes dunes and beaches. It frequently invades sandy fields or pastures and can form nearly pure stands after a few years. Disturbance of the land encourages spread of spotted knapweed, but it can invade undisturbed dunes and other natural communities even in the absence of disturbance.
Spotted knapweed appears to produce substances that inhibit the growth of other plants nearby (it is therefore said to be "allelopathic"). It is also unpalatable to most animals and it is not controllable by fire. Development of biological controls is underway and some success has been achieved through repeated mowing or hand cutting or pulling of plants, but it must be a dedicated, continuous program applied over several years--until the seed bank has been exhausted. Instructions for chemical control (and other methods as well) can be found at several locations on the web.   
As is the case for most invasive species, the best management is to monitor on a regular basis and to find and destroy new populations when they are small. Small populations can be hand pulled or the flower heads removed until the population is eliminated. People working at control of spotted knapweed are advised to wear sturdy gloves, as there is some suspicion that repeated contact with the plants can be hazardous.

## Appearance
Spotted knapweed is a winter-hardy herbaceous weed that typically grows as a perennial or (less commonly)as a biennial. Plants grow 1–3½ ft (0.3–1 m) tall, often have numerous spreading branches, and are supported by a deep taproot. Stems are ridged and covered in small hairs. Leaves are up to 8 in (20 cm) long, gray-green, woolly, and deeply divided near the plant base. Flower heads are produced at the tips of stems and branches. They are ≤½ in (1¼ cm) in diameter, have rows of fringed bracts with dark tips, and have several lavender or pink florets. Each floret produces a single brown seed topped by a tuft of bristly hairs. This plant reproduces only by seed.

# spotted knapweed (Centaurea stoebe australis (Pancic ex A.Kern.) Greuter) - EDDMapS
## Impact
Knapweeds currently infest millions of acres across North America, primarily occurring in rangelands, open forests, pastures, roadsides, vacant lots, and other disturbed areas. They are responsible for millions of dollars of damage annually in reduced agricultural yields and lowered forage value in grazing systems. Knapweeds also displace native vegetation, negatively impacting wildlife and threatening the delicate ecological balance within many habitats. Allelopathic chemicals have been isolated from North American knapweeds, though their role in plant competition is currently under debate.

## Appearance
Spotted knapweed is a winter-hardy herbaceous weed that typically grows as a perennial or (less commonly)as a biennial. Plants grow 1–3½ ft (0.3–1 m) tall, often have numerous spreading branches, and are supported by a deep taproot. Stems are ridged and covered in small hairs. Leaves are up to 8 in (20 cm) long, gray-green, woolly, and deeply divided near the plant base. Flower heads are produced at the tips of stems and branches. They are ≤½ in (1¼ cm) in diameter, have rows of fringed bracts with dark tips, and have several lavender or pink florets. Each floret produces a single brown seed topped by a tuft of bristly hairs. This plant reproduces only by seed.

## Impact
Knapweeds currently infest millions of acres across North America, primarily occurring in rangelands, open forests, pastures, roadsides, vacant lots, and other disturbed areas. They are responsible for millions of dollars of damage annually in reduced agricultural yields and lowered forage value in grazing systems. Knapweeds also displace native vegetation, negatively impacting wildlife and threatening the delicate ecological balance within many habitats. Allelopathic chemicals have been isolated from North American knapweeds, though their role in plant competition is currently under debate.

Spotted knapweed is a serious invader of sunny sites and is especially troublesome in Wisconsin on sandy sites of low productivity, including grasslands, barrens and great lakes dunes and beaches. It frequently invades sandy fields or pastures and can form nearly pure stands after a few years. Disturbance of the land encourages spread of spotted knapweed, but it can invade undisturbed dunes and other natural communities even in the absence of disturbance.
Spotted knapweed appears to produce substances that inhibit the growth of other plants nearby (it is therefore said to be "allelopathic"). It is also unpalatable to most animals and it is not controllable by fire. Development of biological controls is underway and some success has been achieved through repeated mowing or hand cutting or pulling of plants, but it must be a dedicated, continuous program applied over several years--until the seed bank has been exhausted. Instructions for chemical control (and other methods as well) can be found at several locations on the web.   
As is the case for most invasive species, the best management is to monitor on a regular basis and to find and destroy new populations when they are small. Small populations can be hand pulled or the flower heads removed until the population is eliminated. People working at control of spotted knapweed are advised to wear sturdy gloves, as there is some suspicion that repeated contact with the plants can be hazardous.
